newsitem.title: UK: Funds cut Europe equities, raise bonds - poll.
newsitem.headline: Funds cut Europe equities, raise bonds - poll.

text.p: Global fund managers are cutting European equity holdings and raising allocations to European bonds amid widespread concern that stock valuations in developed markets are at unsustainable levels.

A Reuters monthly global asset allocation survey of mostly UK-based fund managers showed a cut in equity holdings across all of Europe, including the UK, with Latin America and emerging markets absorbing most of the flow.

"With uncertainty over EMU, Latin America, which is in the early stages of restructuring with low price/earnings levels is looking increasingly good," said Tony Robinson, head of equities at Lombard Odier.

Fund managers cut back on Europe across the board, with allocations in France at 3.7 percent of a global equity portfolio from 4.3 percent in May, in Germany at 5.4 percent from 5.5 percent and in other Europe to 14.7 percent from 15.6 percent.
Latin America and emerging markets rose for the fourth straight month, rising to 6.5 percent from 4.7 percent.
Disenchantment with European equity markets is partly a reflection of concern about equity market valuations in all developed markets, strategists said.
"The thing that frightens me is the extent to which stock markets have gone up," said Nick Knight, global strategist at Nomura International.
"Its less the relativities one to another that is the problem but the relativities to cash. I'm very nervous that the music is going to stop and I am going to be left holding the baby," he said.
But despite this, few managers are willing to increase their cash holdings, with cash in equity portfolios cut in June to 4.8 percent from 5.7 percent in May.
"I can't hold cash because the markets keep going up, no one wants to be the first one out," said Knight.
UK fund managers slightly increased their underweight position in U.S. equities in June, to 26.5 percent from 25.2 percent in May.
Matthew Merritt, global strategist at ING Barings thinks that U.S. equities may have further to run - but only under very specific conditions.

"Upside potential is critically reliant on the interest rate environment remaining friendly in the U.S. It is important that we see moderation in economic activity which will allow lingering fears of rate hikes to die away," he said.
If that happens, then U.S. equities may have another six to eight percent appreciation in store, with a moderating economy serving as a cap.
Merritt sees U.S. long bonds at 6.50 percent fair value later in the year, with further gains possible in 1998.
Global bond funds increased their holdings in German and non-core European issues in June, largely as a means to hedge risk associated with EMU uncertainty, analysts said.
Funds allocated to German bonds rose to 11.1 percent in June from 9.8 percent in May and non-core European bonds rose to 20.0 percent in June from 16.9 percent in May.
"It has to be Germany as a safe haven for bonds," said Mike Grimble, chief strategist at Norwich Union Investment Management.
Market consensus on EMU is that it will be broad and on time, according to Merritt.
"That provides a marginally higher core long rate and caps potential fall of core long term rates. On convergence plays, Italy is the place where that story still has further to run," he said.

UK pension fund money managers shifted money into local bonds and away from stocks in the month, largely on concerns that Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) may be reduced or abolished in the upcoming July 2 budget.
In June, pension fund managers allocated 57.0 percent of holdings to UK equities, down from 57.8 percent in May and 9.2 percent to gilts, up from 7.9 percent in May, according to the survey.
ACT encourages non-profits such as pension funds to hold equities by excluding dividend payments from taxation.
According to Knight of Nomura, UK gilts are a prime play right now.
"We have changed long term inflation risk in Britain dramatically in the past ten years and its not fully reflected in prices yet," he said.
He believes that UK equities will suffer in the runup to the budget, but may not be too hard hit in the medium-term, especially if changes to ACT are phased in gradually.
"This is the classic case of selling the rumour and buying the fact. When (Chancellor Gordon Brown) stands up -- buy equities, it'll have been discounted by then." - London newsroom +171 542 2734
